title: How Best To Inform Students Of A Consequence https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/03/17/how-best-to-inform-students-of-a-consequence/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the manner in which a teacher delivers a consequence is as important as the consequence itself, since it determines whether responsibility lands with the student or the teacher. He offers a set of guidelines: state clearly why the consequence was given, withhold added commentary or lecturing, don't escort students to time-out, keep tone and body language matter-of-fact, act more like a referee than a judge, protect the teacher-student relationship by avoiding emotional reactions, and move on quickly. He frames these as small but consequential details that, done with 'Oscar-level performance,' ensure students feel the full weight of their own responsibility rather than blaming the teacher.
points: How a consequence is delivered — tone, body language, and wording — is as important to its effectiveness as the consequence itself.
Consequences should be stated clearly and matter-of-factly, without added lectures, scolding, or commentary that shifts blame onto the teacher.
Students should not be escorted to time-out; walking there themselves reinforces their ownership of the misbehavior.
Teachers are encouraged to act 'more like a referee, less like a judge,' enforcing rules impersonally rather than mediating disputes.
The interaction of informing a student of a consequence should take no more than 10-15 seconds before the teacher moves on.
quotes: Whether you’re giving a warning, a time-out, or a letter to take home, the key is to inform them in a way that takes the focus off you—the mere deliverer of the news—and places the responsibility solely with them.
Let your agreed-upon consequence be the only consequence. Refrain from adding a talking-to, a scolding, or your two-cents worth.
A referee’s job is to enforce rules, not mediate disagreements—which makes being fair, consistent, and composed a lot easier.
As soon as you’ve informed the misbehaving student what rule was broken and the consequence, turn your attention back to what you were doing without skipping a beat.

Because if after receiving a consequence your students blame you, or become angry with you, then the consequence will be ineffective. They must see that they alone bear the responsibility for their misbehavior.
